youtube.baslik: Earmolds: Impressions, Materials, Acoustic Changes | Lesson 185 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
The earmold is where the hearing aid meets the ear. In this lesson we cover safe impression taking with an otoblock, acrylic, silicone and vinyl materials, vent types, and how horns and dampers change the frequency response.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Dillon, Hearing Aids; Mueller, Ricketts and Bentler, Modern Hearing Aids; British Society of Audiology, Recommended Procedure: Taking Aural Impressions; American Academy of Audiology, Clinical Practice Guidelines: Pediatric Amplification (2013); Social Security Institution, Health Implementation Communiqué (SUT), Türkiye.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn about the bridge between the hearing aid and the ear: the earmold.
We will see safe impression taking with an otoblock, earmold materials, and how vents, horns and dampers change the sound.
The earmold is the part made from an impression of the person's ear that delivers the aid's sound into the ear canal.
Its first job is to hold the aid or tubing securely in place in the ear.
Its second job is to seal the ear canal well enough to prevent sound leakage and feedback.
Its third job is to deliver sound toward the tympanic membrane through the sound bore inside the earmold.
Its fourth job is to shape the frequency response with modifications such as vents, horns and dampers.
Finally, the earmold must be comfortable enough not to cause pain or pressure when worn all day.

notlar.metin: RIC: the receiver sits in the canal

cumleler: In a classic behind-the-ear aid, sound comes out of the receiver in the case and passes first into the earhook.
After the earhook, a flexible tube with an inner diameter of about 2 mm carries the sound to the earmold.
The tube passes through the earmold and opens into the ear canal; the length and diameter of this section also affect the sound.
In receiver-in-canal aids, however, the receiver sits in the ear canal; the earmold only holds the receiver and seals the canal.
This is why tubing modifications such as horns and dampers are used mostly with classic behind-the-ear systems.
Taking an ear impression is one of the procedures an audiologist performs that demands the most care.
The first step is otoscopy: the shape of the ear canal, wax, discharge and the state of the tympanic membrane are assessed.
Then a cotton or foam block with a thread attached, called an otoblock, is placed in the ear canal.
Using a lighted instrument, the otoblock is advanced to just past the second bend and does not touch the tympanic membrane.
After placement, look again with the otoscope; the otoblock must seal the ear canal without leaving gaps.
The impression material is injected with a syringe or gun, tip held near the otoblock, filling from the inside out without gaps.
Once the material sets, the impression is gently rotated out; finally, the ear canal is checked once more with the otoscope.
The otoblock's job is to stop impression material from reaching the tympanic membrane.
The ear canal has an outer cartilaginous and an inner bony portion, and it makes two bends.
The otoblock is placed just past the second bend, where the bony portion begins.
This way the impression carries the information needed for the earmold to reach deep enough into the ear canal.
A very shallow impression gives an earmold that leaks and is prone to feedback; a block too close to the eardrum is risky.
The block size is chosen to suit the ear canal; a block that is too small lets material leak past its edge.
If there is discharge or a sign of infection in the ear canal, no impression is taken and the person is referred to a physician.
If a perforation of the tympanic membrane is suspected, no impression is taken either; a physician's assessment is awaited.
In ears that have had mastoid surgery the cavity can be large; the block and the amount of material are chosen very carefully.
If wax is blocking the ear canal, it must first be removed appropriately.
If pain, dizziness or coughing occurs during the procedure, stop and check the ear again.
These rules look simple, but the most serious risk of impression taking is material reaching the middle ear.

maddeler.metin: Jaw movement changes the ear canal
Recommended for deep and in-the-ear aids
Material: silicone or powder and liquid

cumleler: When we talk and chew, the jaw joint moves and the cartilaginous portion of the ear canal changes shape.
An impression taken with the mouth closed can give an earmold that loosens and whistles during speech.
So in some cases the person bites on a bite block and an open-mouth impression is taken.
This method is often recommended especially for deeply seated earmolds and in-the-ear aids.
The impression material is usually a two-part silicone or an acrylic-based material mixed from powder and liquid.
Silicone impressions shrink less and can be stored without distortion before they are sent to the laboratory.
Earmold materials differ in hardness, durability and biocompatibility.
Acrylic is hard and durable; it can easily be modified by grinding or drilling a vent, and it is easy to insert.
Silicone is soft and grips the ear canal well, so it is often chosen for a good seal at high gain.
On the other hand, grinding soft silicone or adding a vent later is more difficult.
Vinyl is soft and comfortable, but over time it can shrink, harden and change color.
Materials such as polyethylene, and some silicones, are used as options for people with material allergies.
For children, soft materials are usually preferred so that the earmold is comfortable and does not injure the ear on impact.
Because severe loss requires high gain, a soft earmold that seals the ear canal tightly reduces feedback.
For an older user with reduced dexterity and vision, a hard, smooth earmold can make insertion easier.
If itching, redness or swelling appears, a material allergy is considered and a compatible material is used instead.
So there is no single best material; the choice depends on the person's ear, hearing loss and daily life.

maddeler.metin: Parallel vent: separate from sound bore
A vent can be enlarged later

cumleler: A vent is a second channel running from the outer surface of the earmold into the ear canal; we saw its effect in the previous lesson.
The most common type, the parallel vent, runs parallel to the sound bore and separate from it.
If space is tight, a diagonal vent that joins the sound bore can be used, but it can also cause gain loss at high frequencies.
This is why a diagonal vent is avoided, especially for people for whom high-frequency gain is important.
A very small pressure vent ventilates the ear canal and equalizes pressure while barely affecting the sound.
In an acrylic earmold a vent can be widened later; different sizes can also be tried with interchangeable vent plugs.
An acoustic horn is a sound bore that gradually widens toward the ear canal.
When a tube opens from a narrow end to a wide end, high-frequency sounds are delivered into the ear canal more efficiently.

cumleler.yazi: The classic example is the Libby horn, which widens from about 2 mm to 4 mm.

cumleler: In this example, the horn raises output by about 7 dB above 2500 Hz.
Sources usually give this boost as about 6 to 10 dB; the earmold length and the ear canal change the result.
Conversely, a reverse horn that narrows toward the ear canal reduces output at high frequencies.
The tubing and receiver system creates marked peaks in the frequency response through its own resonances.
In this example, three peaks are seen around 1000, 3000 and 5000 Hz.
An acoustic damper is a small filter placed in the sound path that resists the flow of sound.
The damper flattens the peaks and makes the response smoother.
A smoother response reduces sudden discomfort with loud sounds and can increase the margin before feedback.
Dampers come in different resistance values; the higher the value, the more the peaks are suppressed.
Now let us see the acoustic modifications together.
As the vent gets larger, gain decreases at low frequencies and the occlusion effect eases.
A horn increases output at high frequencies.
A reverse horn, by contrast, reduces output at high frequencies.
A damper does not target a particular region; it flattens the curve by suppressing the peaks in the response.

maddeler.metin: Replace tubing that hardens or yellows

cumleler: Wipe the earmold daily with a dry cloth; removable earmolds can be washed in warm soapy water per the maker's advice, then dried well.
If the sound bore or vent is blocked with wax, the sound weakens; so cleaning with a small brush and wire is taught.
Over time the tubing hardens, yellows or cracks; it usually needs replacing every few months.
Because the ear grows quickly in infants, the American Academy of Audiology pediatric guideline notes earmolds may need replacing monthly.
In Türkiye, the Social Security Institution covers an earmold every 6 months under age 13 and once a year from age 13.
Under the same regulation, no separate earmold fee is paid with the first aid; these rules can change, so check the current regulation.

sahneler.metin: Inspect the impression before sending it to the lab: a smooth otoblock end, a surface without voids and a clear second bend. A flawed impression means a flawed earmold.
cumleler: A tip from the field: after removing the impression, always inspect it in your hand before sending it to the laboratory.
The otoblock end should look smooth at the tip of the impression, and the second bend should be clearly visible.
If there are air bubbles, cracks or voids on the surface, the earmold will not sit fully in the ear canal and will leak.
Parts such as the concha and the helix root must also be complete, because these are the parts that hold the earmold in the ear.
Redoing a doubtful impression takes a few minutes; a flawed earmold means weeks of whistling and discomfort.

maddeler.metin: Otoblock just past the second bend
Hard acrylic, soft silicone and vinyl
Vent lows, horn highs; damper peaks

cumleler: In this lesson we saw that the earmold holds the aid, seals the ear canal, delivers sound and shapes the response.
Otoscopy is essential for a safe impression, and the otoblock goes just past the second bend without touching the eardrum.
Acrylic is hard and easy to modify; silicone and vinyl are soft and often preferred for children.
A vent reduces low-frequency gain, a horn increases high-frequency output, and a damper suppresses peaks in the response.

sahneler.soru: Which is used to increase high-frequency output?
sahneler.aciklama: A horn _widens_ the sound bore toward the ear canal and delivers high-frequency sounds more efficiently.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: in a classic behind-the-ear aid, which earmold modification increases output at high frequencies?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: a horn.
A sound bore that widens toward the ear canal delivers highs more efficiently; a reverse horn and a diagonal vent reduce the highs.
